questions.q: For real numbers a and b, exactly one of a < b, a = b or a > b is true. What is this property of real numbers called?
questions.x: Exactly one of the three order relations holds: this is the trichotomy property. Transitivity says a < b and b < c give a < c; closure says an operation keeps results inside the set.

questions.q: In the 8-row truth table for the statements p, q and r, in how many rows is (p → q) ∧ (q → r) true?
questions.x: Both implications hold exactly when no true letter is followed by a false one in the order p, q, r: FFF, FFT, FTT and TTT. That is 4 rows; for example TFT fails because p → q is false there.

questions.q: f(x) = |x| and g(x) = x − 3. What is f(g(−1)) + g(f(−1))?
questions.x: g(−1) = −4, so f(g(−1)) = |−4| = 4; f(−1) = 1, so g(f(−1)) = 1 − 3 = −2. The sum is 4 + (−2) = 2. Forgetting the absolute value gives −4 − 2 = −6.

questions.q: lim(x→0) (tan x − sin x)/x³ equals:
questions.x: tan x − sin x = sin x(1 − cos x)/cos x, so the expression is (sin x/x)·((1 − cos x)/x²)·(1/cos x) → 1 · ½ · 1 = ½. Replacing tan x and sin x both by x too early gives the wrong value 0.

questions.q: The parabola y = ax² + bx + c passes through (1, 2), (2, 3) and (−1, 6). What is c?
questions.x: a + b + c = 2, 4a + 2b + c = 3, a − b + c = 6. First minus third: 2b = −4, so b = −2; second minus first: 3a + b = 1, so a = 1; then c = 2 − 1 + 2 = 3. Check (2, 3): 4 − 4 + 3 = 3.

questions.q: For which value of θ is the matrix [[cos θ, sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]] singular?
questions.x: The determinant is cos²θ − sin²θ = cos 2θ, which is 0 when 2θ = π/2, i.e. θ = π/4. At θ = π/2 it is cos π = −1, and at π/3 and π/6 it is −½ and ½.

questions.q: What is the minimum value of 2x² + 8x + 3?
questions.x: 2x² + 8x + 3 = 2(x + 2)² − 8 + 3 = 2(x + 2)² − 5, so the minimum is −5 at x = −2. Check: 2(4) − 16 + 3 = −5. Forgetting the factor 2 when completing the square gives −13.

questions.q: Which point satisfies both equations y = 2x and x² + y² = 20?
questions.x: Substituting y = 2x: x² + 4x² = 20, so x = ±2, giving (2, 4) and (−2, −4). Only (2, 4) is in the list. (4, 2) lies on the circle but not on y = 2x.

questions.q: The angles of a triangle are in A.P. and the smallest angle is 40°. What is the largest angle?
questions.x: Write the angles as a − d, a, a + d. Their sum 3a = 180°, so a = 60°; a − d = 40° gives d = 20°, and the largest is 80°. Check: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180°. 60° is the middle angle.

questions.q: What is the 7th term of the G.P. √2, 2, 2√2, … ?
questions.x: a = √2 and r = 2/√2 = √2, so a₇ = ar⁶ = √2 × (√2)⁶ = √2 × 8 = 8√2. Check: the terms run √2, 2, 2√2, 4, 4√2, 8, 8√2. Using r⁷ gives 16.

questions.q: The letters of the word EQUAL are arranged in a row. In how many arrangements do the vowels occupy the 1st, 3rd and 5th places?
questions.x: The vowels E, U, A fill the three odd places in 3! = 6 ways and the consonants Q, L fill the two even places in 2! = 2 ways: 6 × 2 = 12. Counting only the vowels gives 6.

questions.q: Which of these powers of x occurs in the expansion of (x − 1/x)¹⁰?
questions.x: The general term is ¹⁰Cᵣ x^(10 − r)(−1/x)ʳ = (−1)ʳ ¹⁰Cᵣ x^(10 − 2r). So only even powers from x¹⁰ down to x⁻¹⁰ occur; 10 − 2r = 4 at r = 3, while 5, 3 and −7 are odd.

questions.q: A sector of a circle has arc length 6 cm and area 15 cm². What is its central angle?
questions.x: Area = ½ r l gives 15 = ½ × r × 6, so r = 5 cm. Then θ = l/r = 6/5 rad. Inverting the ratio gives 5/6 rad.

questions.q: What is the value of sin 75° sin 15°?
questions.x: 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) = cos 60° − cos 90° = 1/2, so sin 75° sin 15° = 1/4. Forgetting to halve gives 1/2.

questions.q: As x varies, what is the greatest value of y = sin x + sin(x + 2π/3) + sin(x + 4π/3)?
questions.x: sin(x + 2π/3) + sin(x + 4π/3) = 2 sin(x + π) cos(π/3) = −sin x, so y = 0 for every x and its greatest value is 0. 3 assumes all three sines reach 1 together.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, A = 30°, B = 60° and the circumradius R = 5. What is the inradius r?
questions.x: C = 90°, so c = 2R = 10, a = 2R sin 30° = 5 and b = 2R sin 60° = 5√3. For a right triangle r = (a + b − c)/2 = (5√3 − 5)/2 = 5(√3 − 1)/2. Check: Δ = 25√3/2 and s = (15 + 5√3)/2, and Δ/s gives the same value.

questions.q: A kite is flying on a straight string 100 m long that makes an angle of 30° with the level ground. How high is the kite above the ground?
questions.x: The height is opposite the 30° angle and the string is the hypotenuse, so h = 100 sin 30° = 50 m. Using cos 30° gives 50√3 m, the horizontal distance.

questions.q: The solutions of sec θ + tan θ = √3 in the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π are:
questions.x: Multiply by cos θ: 1 + sin θ = √3 cos θ, so √3 cos θ − sin θ = 1, i.e. 2 cos(θ + π/6) = 1, giving θ = π/6 or 3π/2. At 3π/2, cos θ = 0 and sec θ, tan θ are undefined, so reject it. Check π/6: 2/√3 + 1/√3 = √3.

questions.q: What is the derivative of y = ln(cosh x)?
questions.x: d/dx ln(cosh x) = (sinh x)/(cosh x) = tanh x, since d/dx cosh x = +sinh x (no minus sign, unlike cos x). Inverting the fraction gives coth x.

questions.q: The tangent to the curve y = f(x) at x = 1 is the line 2x + y = 5. What is f′(1)?
questions.x: f′(1) is the slope of the tangent at x = 1. Writing the line as y = −2x + 5 shows its slope is −2. Forgetting the sign when solving for y gives 2.

questions.q: ∫ (sin x)/cos²x dx, for |x| < π/2, equals:
questions.x: sin x/cos²x = (1/cos x)(sin x/cos x) = sec x tan x, whose antiderivative is sec x + C. Check: d/dx (cos x)⁻¹ = −(cos x)⁻²(−sin x) = sin x/cos²x. Losing that double minus sign gives −sec x.

questions.q: ∫ (1 + x)²/√x dx, for x > 0, equals:
questions.x: Expand and divide: x^(−1/2) + 2x^(1/2) + x^(3/2). Integrating term by term gives 2x^(1/2) + (4/3)x^(3/2) + (2/5)x^(5/2) + C. Forgetting the middle factor 2 gives (2/3)x^(3/2).

questions.q: ∫₀¹ x(1 − x)⁹ dx equals:
questions.x: Using ∫₀¹ f(x) dx = ∫₀¹ f(1 − x) dx, the integral equals ∫₀¹ (1 − x)x⁹ dx = 1/10 − 1/11 = 1/110. The substitution u = 1 − x gives the same: ∫₀¹ (1 − u)u⁹ du.

questions.q: What is the area of the parallelogram bounded by the lines x + 2y = 0, x + 2y = 5, 2x − y = 0 and 2x − y = 10?
questions.x: The two pairs of lines are perpendicular, so the figure is a rectangle. Its sides are the distances between the parallel lines: 5/√5 = √5 and 10/√5 = 2√5. Area = √5 × 2√5 = 10.

questions.q: Which point lies on one of the lines represented by 2x² − 3xy − 2y² = 0?
questions.x: 2x² − 3xy − 2y² = (2x + y)(x − 2y), so the lines are 2x + y = 0 and x = 2y, and (2, 1) lies on x = 2y. Check by substitution: 8 − 6 − 2 = 0.

questions.q: Maximise z = 2x + 3y subject to x + y ≤ 6, x ≤ 4, y ≤ 5, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. What is the maximum value of z?
questions.x: Corner points (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 2), (1, 5), (0, 5) give z = 0, 8, 14, 17, 15. The maximum is 17 at (1, 5). Ignoring y ≤ 5 and using (0, 6) gives 18.

questions.q: What is the equation of the tangent to the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 at its point (x₁, y₁)?
questions.x: Replace x² by xx₁ and y² by yy₁. Check at the vertex (a, 0): x·a/a² = 1 gives x = a, the vertical tangent there. The minus sign belongs to the hyperbola.

questions.q: The parabola y = ax² + bx + c has its vertex at (1, 2) and passes through (0, 3). What is its focus?
questions.x: y = a(x − 1)² + 2 and y(0) = 3 give a = 1, so (x − 1)² = y − 2. Here 4p = 1, p = ¼, and it opens upward, so the focus is (1, 2 + ¼) = (1, 9/4). Going down by ¼ instead gives (1, 7/4).

questions.q: If [a b c] = a · (b × c) = 5, what is b · (a × c)?
questions.x: b · (a × c) = [b a c], and swapping two vectors changes the sign: [b a c] = −[a b c] = −5. Only cyclic changes such as [b c a] keep the value 5.

questions.q: A particle starts from rest at the origin with acceleration a = 6t − 6 m/s². At what time does it return to the origin?
questions.x: v = 3t² − 6t and s = t³ − 3t² = t²(t − 3), so s = 0 again at t = 3 s. At t = 2 s it is only momentarily at rest, farthest from the origin (s = −4 m).

questions.q: Which of the following is a derived SI unit?
questions.x: The coulomb is defined from base units as 1 C = 1 A s, so it is derived. The ampere, kelvin and candela are all base units; the ampere is tempting because charge and current are linked.

questions.q: Using the right-handed unit vectors î, ĵ and k̂, the vector product k̂ × ĵ is equal to:
questions.x: In cyclic order ĵ × k̂ = î, and reversing the order of a vector product reverses its sign, so k̂ × ĵ = −î. Forgetting the sign change gives î.

questions.q: A very heavy body moving at speed v makes a head-on elastic collision with a very light body at rest. Just after the collision, the light body moves with a speed of about:
questions.x: For a head-on elastic collision, v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂); with m₁ ≫ m₂ this is about 2u₁ = 2v. Check: the heavy body keeps about v, and the relative speed of separation must equal the approach speed v, so the light body moves at v + v = 2v.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal component of a projectile's velocity during its flight:
o: Decreases to zero at the highest point
Changes direction at the highest point
questions.x: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity component stays constant. It is the vertical component that falls to zero at the highest point and then reverses.

questions.q: A force acting along a straight line is +20 N for the first 2 m of displacement and then −10 N (opposite to the motion) for the next 2 m. The net work done by the force over the 4 m is:
questions.x: Work = area under the force–displacement graph, counting area below the axis as negative: 20 × 2 + (−10) × 2 = 40 − 20 = 20 J. Adding both areas as positive gives 60 J; taking only the first part gives 40 J.

questions.q: An electric motor takes in 500 W and lifts a 40 kg load vertically at a steady 1 m s⁻¹. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the efficiency of the motor is:
questions.x: Useful output power = Fv = mgv = 40 × 10 × 1 = 400 W, so efficiency = 400/500 × 100 = 80 %. Inverting the ratio gives an impossible 125 %; leaving out g gives 8 %.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.8 m on a smooth table, held by a string that breaks if the tension exceeds 40 N. The greatest speed the stone can have is:
questions.x: The tension supplies the centripetal force: T = mv²/r, so v² = Tr/m = 40 × 0.8/0.5 = 64 and v = 8 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 64 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: In Bernoulli's equation, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, each term has the dimensions of:
questions.x: Each term has the unit of pressure, N m⁻² = N m/m³ = J m⁻³, which is energy per unit volume (e.g. ½ρv² is kinetic energy per unit volume). Energy per unit mass would need each term divided by ρ.

questions.q: The displacement of a particle is x = 0.04 sin(10πt), with x in metres and t in seconds. The amplitude and frequency of its motion are:
questions.x: Comparing with x = x₀ sin ωt: x₀ = 0.04 m and ω = 10π rad s⁻¹, so f = ω/2π = 5 Hz. Reading ω or the number 10 as the frequency gives the other values; 0.08 m is the peak-to-peak distance.

questions.q: A gas has pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, density 1.4 kg m⁻³ and γ = 1.4. Using Laplace's formula, the speed of sound in it is about:
questions.x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(1.4 × 10⁵/1.4) = √(10⁵) ≈ 316 m s⁻¹. Newton's formula without γ gives √(10⁵/1.4) ≈ 267 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 120 Hz. The frequency of its second overtone is:
questions.x: For a string fixed at both ends the overtones are 2f₁, 3f₁, …; the second overtone is the third harmonic, 3 × 120 = 360 Hz. Taking the second overtone as the second harmonic gives 240 Hz.

questions.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slit separation is halved and the screen is moved to half its original distance from the slits, using the same light. The fringe spacing:
questions.x: Fringe spacing Δy = λL/d. Halving L halves Δy and halving d doubles it, so Δy is unchanged. Taking only one of the two changes gives double or half.

questions.q: Compared with the objective of an astronomical telescope, the objective of a compound microscope has:
o: A long focal length and a large aperture
A long focal length and a small aperture
The same focal length but a larger aperture
A short focal length and a small aperture
questions.x: A microscope objective is close to a tiny nearby object and must give a large real image, so it has a very short focal length and a small aperture. A telescope objective must collect light from distant objects and needs a long focal length and a wide aperture.

questions.q: A gas occupies 3 litres at 27 °C and a pressure of 1 atm. It is heated to 127 °C and compressed to 2 litres. What is its new pressure?
questions.x: p₂ = p₁V₁T₂/(V₂T₁) = 1 × 3 × 400/(2 × 300) = 2.0 atm. Check: compressing alone gives 1.5 atm, and heating from 300 K to 400 K multiplies this by 4/3. Using Celsius temperatures gives 7.1 atm.

questions.q: Which of the following is an assumption of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
o: Collisions of the molecules with each other and with the walls are perfectly elastic
The molecules attract each other strongly
The molecules take up a large part of the container's volume
All the molecules move with the same speed
questions.x: Kinetic theory assumes elastic collisions, negligible molecular volume, no forces except during collisions, and random motion with a spread of speeds. So only the elastic-collision statement is an assumption.

questions.q: Capacitors of 2 μF, 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is:
questions.x: 1/C = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = (3 + 2 + 1)/6 = 1, so C = 1 μF. Adding them, as for parallel, gives 11 μF. A series combination is always smaller than the smallest capacitor.

questions.q: A positive charge and a negative charge are brought closer together. Their electric potential energy:
questions.x: U = kq₁q₂/r is negative for unlike charges, and its size grows as r falls, so U becomes more negative: the field does positive work as they attract.

questions.q: A uniform wire of resistance 12 Ω is bent into a complete circle. The resistance between two points at opposite ends of a diameter is:
questions.x: The two points split the circle into two semicircles of 6 Ω each, in parallel between them: 6 × 6/(6 + 6) = 3 Ω. Taking just one semicircle gives 6 Ω.

questions.q: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series across a 3 Ω resistor, but one cell has been connected the wrong way round. The current in the resistor is:
questions.x: The reversed cell cancels one correct cell, so the net emf is 3 × 1.5 − 1.5 = 3 V, but all four internal resistances (2 Ω) are still in the circuit: I = 3/(3 + 2) = 0.6 A. With all cells aiding, 6/5 = 1.2 A; treating the reversed cell as simply missing gives 4.5/5 = 0.9 A.

questions.q: A charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field. The work done on it by the magnetic force is:
o: Positive, because the force speeds the particle up
Negative, because the force slows the particle down
Zero, because the force is always perpendicular to the velocity
Equal to qvB times the distance moved
questions.x: F = q(v × B) is always at right angles to v, so it does no work (W = Fd cos 90° = 0). The particle's speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only its direction changes.

questions.q: Two air-cored solenoids have the same number of turns per metre and the same cross-sectional area, but solenoid Y is twice as long as solenoid X. The ratio of their self-inductances, L(Y) : L(X), is:
questions.x: L = μ₀N²A/l. Y has twice the length and so twice the turns: L(Y)/L(X) = (2²/2) = 2. Equivalently L = μ₀n²Al with n fixed, so L ∝ l. Squaring the turns without dividing by the doubled length gives 4 : 1.

questions.q: A closed coil of 100 turns, each of area 0.01 m², and total resistance 2 Ω lies at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The field decreases steadily at 0.4 T s⁻¹. The induced current is:
questions.x: ε = NA(ΔB/Δt) = 100 × 0.01 × 0.4 = 0.4 V, and I = ε/R = 0.4/2 = 0.2 A. 0.4 A takes the emf as the current; leaving out N gives 2 × 10⁻³ A.

questions.q: A 0.1 H inductor is to be used with a capacitor in a series circuit that resonates at 50 Hz. The capacitance needed is (take π² ≈ 10):
questions.x: f = 1/(2π√(LC)) gives C = 1/(4π²f²L) = 1/(4 × 10 × 2500 × 0.1) = 1/10 000 F = 100 μF. Check: LC = 10⁻⁵, √(LC) ≈ 3.16 × 10⁻³ s, and 1/(2π × 3.16 × 10⁻³) ≈ 50 Hz. Forgetting to square f leads to a much larger value.

questions.q: A wire 2 m long with cross-sectional area 1 mm² is made of metal with Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa. It is stretched by 2 mm, within its elastic limit. The elastic energy stored in it is:
questions.x: F = YAΔL/L = 2 × 10¹¹ × 1 × 10⁻⁶ × 2 × 10⁻³ / 2 = 200 N, so E = ½FΔL = ½ × 200 × 0.002 = 0.2 J. Check: energy density ½Y(strain)² = ½ × 2 × 10¹¹ × (10⁻³)² = 10⁵ J m⁻³, times volume 2 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 0.2 J. Leaving out the ½ gives 0.4 J; using 2 for the extension in metres gives 200 J.

questions.q: A silicon diode (forward voltage drop 0.7 V) is connected in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5.7 V battery so that the diode is forward biased. The current in the circuit is:
questions.x: The resistor gets 5.7 − 0.7 = 5.0 V, so I = 5.0 V / 1000 Ω = 5 mA. Ignoring the diode's drop gives 5.7 mA; adding it instead of subtracting gives 6.4 mA.

questions.q: According to an observer on the Earth, a clock on a spaceship moving past at a speed close to the speed of light:
o: Keeps the same time as Earth clocks
questions.x: By time dilation t = t₀/√(1 − v²/c²), an interval of the moving clock appears longer to the Earth observer, so the moving clock runs slow. It would stop only at v = c, which a clock cannot reach.

questions.q: A black body at 2000 K radiates most strongly at 1.45 μm. It is heated until it radiates most strongly at 0.725 μm. The total power it radiates becomes:
questions.x: Wien's law λ_max T = constant: halving λ_max means T doubles to 4000 K. By Stefan's law the power ∝ T⁴, so it rises by 2⁴ = 16. Stopping after Wien's law gives 2 times; using λ ∝ T gives ½.

questions.q: The energy levels of hydrogen are Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. As the quantum number n increases, the energy difference between neighbouring levels:
o: Decreases, so the levels crowd together
questions.x: Eₙ ∝ −1/n², so the gaps shrink: E₂ − E₁ = 10.2 eV, E₃ − E₂ = 1.89 eV, E₄ − E₃ = 0.66 eV, and the levels crowd towards the ionisation limit E = 0. They are not equally spaced.

questions.q: The diameter of an atom is of the order of 10⁻¹⁰ m and that of its nucleus is of the order of 10⁻¹⁴ m. The atom is larger than its nucleus by a factor of about:
questions.x: 10⁻¹⁰ / 10⁻¹⁴ = 10⁴, so the atom is about ten thousand times wider than its nucleus. Multiplying the powers gives 10⁻²⁴, and the reciprocal 10⁻⁴ compares the wrong way round.

questions.q: For a PET scan, the patient is given a tracer, such as a sugar labelled with fluorine-18, that collects in active tissue. The radioactive atoms in the tracer emit:
questions.x: PET means positron emission tomography: the tracer emits positrons, each of which meets an electron and annihilates into two gamma-ray photons that travel in opposite directions and are detected. Alpha emitters would be far too damaging inside the body.

questions.q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What mass of magnesium gives 0.1 mol of hydrogen gas? (Mg = 24)
questions.x: Mg : H₂ = 1 : 1, so 0.1 mol Mg is needed = 0.1 × 24 = 2.4 g. Using the 2 in front of HCl doubles or halves the answer to 4.8 g or 1.2 g.

questions.q: A mixture contains iodine, sand and sodium chloride. Which sequence separates all three?
o: Add water and filter; heat the filtrate to sublime the iodine; the residue is sand
Heat gently to sublime the iodine; add water to the residue and filter off the sand; evaporate the filtrate to get the salt
Add water and evaporate; sublime the residue to get the salt; the sand stays behind
Heat strongly to melt the salt; filter off the sand; cool to get iodine crystals
questions.x: Iodine sublimes, so it is removed first by gentle heating; sand is insoluble and salt is soluble, so water and filtration separate them, and evaporation gives the salt. Adding water first dissolves some iodine with the salt, and NaCl does not sublime or melt at a practical temperature.

questions.q: At 0 °C, hydrogen and helium show Z = PV/nRT greater than 1 at all pressures. The reason is that:
o: Their intermolecular attractions are very weak, so the effect of molecular volume dominates
questions.x: H₂ and He are small, non-polar and hardly polarisable, so attractions (which lower Z) are tiny, and the excluded volume (which raises Z) wins. They are among the hardest gases to liquefy.

questions.q: Ice is an example of a:
questions.x: Ice is made of separate H₂O molecules held in the lattice by hydrogen bonds, so it is a molecular solid. The covalent O–H bonds are only inside each molecule, not a continuous network as in diamond.

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons does a nitrogen atom (Z = 7) have in its ground state?
questions.x: N is 1s² 2s² 2p³; by Hund's rule the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, so 3 unpaired electrons. Pairing two of them in one orbital gives 1.

questions.q: In the carbon monoxide molecule, C and O are joined by a triple bond. How is this triple bond made up?
o: Two normal covalent bonds and one coordinate covalent bond donated by oxygen
Three normal covalent bonds, each with one electron from C and one from O
One normal covalent bond and two coordinate covalent bonds donated by carbon
Two normal covalent bonds and one ionic bond
questions.x: Carbon has 4 and oxygen 6 valence electrons. Two pairs are shared normally (2 electrons from each atom), and oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to carbon as a coordinate bond, giving :C≡O: with an octet on both. Three normal bonds would need three electrons from oxygen and three from carbon and leave carbon short of an octet.

questions.q: The dipole moment of a polar bond is defined as:
o: The difference in electronegativity of the two bonded atoms
The energy needed to break the bond into atoms
The ratio of the partial charge to the bond length
The product of the magnitude of the partial charge and the distance between the charges
questions.x: μ = q × r, so it has units of charge × length (C m, or debye). Electronegativity difference decides whether there is a dipole and roughly how big it is, but is not the dipole moment itself.

questions.q: For a reaction, ΔH = −100 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −200 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, both roughly constant with temperature. Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, which statement is correct?
o: It is spontaneous at 600 K but not at 300 K
It is spontaneous at both 300 K and 600 K
It is spontaneous at neither 300 K nor 600 K
It is spontaneous at 300 K but not at 600 K
questions.x: With ΔS = −0.200 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: at 300 K, ΔG = −100 + 60 = −40 kJ mol⁻¹ (spontaneous); at 600 K, ΔG = −100 + 120 = +20 kJ mol⁻¹ (not spontaneous). Forgetting to convert J to kJ makes the TΔS term tiny and suggests 'spontaneous at both'.

questions.q: An equilibrium mixture of N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) in a 2.0 dm³ vessel contains 0.40 mol of N₂O₄ and 0.40 mol of NO₂. What is Kc?
questions.x: Concentrations: [N₂O₄] = [NO₂] = 0.40 ÷ 2.0 = 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Kc = [NO₂]² / [N₂O₄] = 0.040 ÷ 0.20 = 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Using moles instead of concentrations gives 0.16 ÷ 0.40 = 0.40; forgetting the square gives 1.0.

questions.q: Calcium oxide reacts with sulphur trioxide: CaO + SO₃ → CaSO₄. In the Lewis sense, which species acts as the acid?
o: O²⁻, which donates an electron pair
Ca²⁺, which donates an electron pair
SO₃, which accepts an electron pair from the oxide ion
CaSO₄, which is formed from the acid
questions.x: The oxide ion O²⁻ of CaO donates a lone pair to the sulphur atom of SO₃, forming SO₄²⁻; the electron-pair acceptor, SO₃, is the Lewis acid and O²⁻ is the Lewis base. No proton is transferred, so the reaction is an acid–base reaction only in the Lewis sense.

questions.q: What mass of ethylene glycol, C₂H₆O₂ (molar mass 62 g mol⁻¹), must be dissolved in 500 g of water to lower its freezing point to −3.72 °C? (Kf of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
questions.x: ΔTf = Kf × m, so m = 3.72/1.86 = 2.0 mol kg⁻¹. In 0.500 kg of water that is 1.0 mol, i.e. 62 g. Forgetting that only 500 g of water is used gives 124 g.

questions.q: The discharge reaction of a lead storage battery is Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. What mass of H₂SO₄ is used up when the battery delivers 0.50 F of charge? (H₂SO₄ = 98 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: As written, Pb goes from 0 to +2 and Pb in PbO₂ from +4 to +2, so 2 electrons pass for 2 mol H₂SO₄: 1 mol H₂SO₄ per faraday. 0.50 F uses 0.50 mol = 49 g. Taking 1 electron per equation doubles this to 98 g.

questions.q: Molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr₂, is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What is formed at the cathode?
questions.x: The cathode is negative and reduces cations: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. Bromine forms at the anode. With no water present, hydrogen and oxygen cannot form.

questions.q: The rate equation of a reaction is rate = k[X]²[Y], with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and time in seconds. What is the unit of k?
questions.x: k = rate/([X]²[Y]) = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)³ = mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹. dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ is the unit for a second-order reaction; this one is third order overall.

questions.q: Five consecutive elements of period 3, V, W, X, Y and Z (in order of increasing atomic number), have first ionisation energies 578, 787, 1012, 1000 and 1251 kJ mol⁻¹. To which group does Y belong?
questions.x: Across period 3 the ionisation energy dips twice: from group 2 to 13 and from group 15 to 16. The pattern here is rise, rise, fall, rise; starting at Na or Mg would put a fall in the wrong place, so V to Z are Al, Si, P, S and Cl. Y is sulphur, group 16; X is phosphorus (group 15), the tempting answer.

questions.q: The main reason for the anomalous behaviour of lithium compared with the other alkali metals is its:
o: Very small atomic and ionic size, which gives Li⁺ a high polarising power
questions.x: The tiny Li atom and Li⁺ ion give a high charge density, so lithium's compounds are more covalent and its behaviour resembles magnesium. Lithium has the smallest radius and the highest ionisation energy in the group, and it forms only Li⁺.

questions.q: White lead, once widely used as a white paint pigment, is:
questions.x: White lead is basic lead carbonate, 2PbCO₃·Pb(OH)₂. Pb₃O₄ is red lead, PbCrO₄ is the yellow pigment chrome yellow, and PbO₂ is a dark brown oxide; red lead is the usual mix-up.

questions.q: White phosphorus is converted into red phosphorus by:
o: Burning it in a limited supply of air
Dissolving it in carbon disulphide and evaporating the solvent
Boiling it with sodium hydroxide solution
Heating it to about 250 °C in the absence of air
questions.x: Heating white phosphorus at about 250 °C out of contact with air links the P₄ units into polymeric red phosphorus. Burning gives oxides, CS₂ only recrystallises white phosphorus, and NaOH gives phosphine.

questions.q: Fe³⁺ combines with three oxalate ions, C₂O₄²⁻ (a bidentate ligand), to form a complex ion. The charge on the complex ion and the coordination number of iron are:
questions.x: Charge = +3 + 3(−2) = −3, giving [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻; each oxalate uses two donor atoms, so the coordination number is 3 × 2 = 6. Counting ligands instead of donor atoms gives 3.

questions.q: Which statement about cis- and trans-1,2-dichloroethene is correct?
o: The cis isomer has a net dipole moment and the higher boiling point
The trans isomer has a net dipole moment and the higher boiling point
Both have the same boiling point because they have the same molecular formula
Both have zero dipole moment because they have the same bonds
questions.x: In the cis isomer both C–Cl dipoles point to the same side and add up, so it is polar and boils higher (about 60 °C); in the trans isomer they point opposite ways and cancel (about 48 °C). Thinking the more symmetrical trans form is more polar is the slip.

questions.q: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl and CH₃CHClCH₃ are examples of:
questions.x: Both have the same carbon chain and the same functional group; only the position of the Cl on the chain differs, so they are position isomers. The carbon skeleton is unchanged, which rules out chain isomerism.

questions.q: 1,1,2,2-Tetrabromoethane, Br₂CHCHBr₂, is heated with excess zinc dust. The organic product is:
questions.x: Each zinc atom removes two bromine atoms from neighbouring carbons; with excess zinc all four go and a triple bond forms: Br₂CHCHBr₂ + 2Zn → HC≡CH + 2ZnBr₂. Removing only two Br would give 1,2-dibromoethene, not ethene.

questions.q: Hydrogenation of cyclohexa-1,3-diene to cyclohexane releases 232 kJ mol⁻¹, and hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane releases 208 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for C₆H₆ + H₂ → cyclohexa-1,3-diene?
questions.x: By Hess's law, ΔH(benzene → diene) = ΔH(benzene → cyclohexane) − ΔH(diene → cyclohexane) = −208 − (−232) = +24 kJ mol⁻¹. Adding the first H₂ is uphill because it destroys the aromatic ring's stability; subtracting the other way round gives −24.

questions.q: Which compound CANNOT be used to prepare a stable Grignard reagent by reaction with magnesium in dry ether?
questions.x: A Grignard reagent is destroyed by any acidic hydrogen. In BrCH₂CH₂OH the –OH of the molecule itself would protonate the C–Mg carbon as soon as it formed. The other three have no O–H or N–H group; aryl and secondary halides form Grignard reagents normally.

questions.q: Sodium ethoxide, C₂H₅ONa, is added to water. It reacts to form ethanol and sodium hydroxide. This shows that:
o: Ethanol is a stronger acid than water
The ethoxide ion is a weaker base than the hydroxide ion
Sodium ethoxide is an oxidising agent
Ethanol is a weaker acid than water
questions.x: C₂H₅O⁻ takes H⁺ from H₂O, so the reaction goes to the weaker acid (ethanol) and weaker base (OH⁻). Ethoxide is therefore the stronger base, and ethanol the weaker acid. Reading the equation backwards gives the tempting wrong choices.

questions.q: Ethanal reacts with HCN (with a trace of base), and the product is then hydrolysed by heating with dilute acid. The final organic product is:
questions.x: CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon to give the cyanohydrin CH₃CH(OH)CN; acid hydrolysis turns –CN into –COOH on the same carbon. Propanoic acid forgets the –OH; 3-hydroxy puts the groups on different carbons.

questions.q: A mixture of glycine (pI 6.0), lysine (pI 9.7) and aspartic acid (pI 2.8) is placed at the centre of an electrophoresis strip in a buffer of pH 6.0, and a voltage is applied. What happens?
o: Lysine moves to the anode, aspartic acid to the cathode, glycine stays near the start
Aspartic acid moves to the anode, lysine to the cathode, glycine stays near the start
All three move to the cathode at different speeds
Glycine moves to the anode, lysine to the cathode, aspartic acid stays near the start
questions.x: At a pH above its pI an amino acid is negative and moves to the anode (aspartic acid); below its pI it is positive and moves to the cathode (lysine); at its pI it has no net charge (glycine). Reversing the rule (pH above pI means positive) gives the swapped option.

questions.q: A double-stranded DNA segment has 10 base pairs, of which 4 are guanine–cytosine pairs and the rest are adenine–thymine pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together in this segment?
questions.x: G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs by two: 4 × 3 + 6 × 2 = 12 + 12 = 24. Giving every pair two bonds gives 20 and every pair three gives 30; swapping the counts for the two kinds of pair gives 26.

questions.q: A compound C₃H₆O₂ shows a strong IR band near 1730 cm⁻¹ and no broad band anywhere between 2500 and 3600 cm⁻¹. The compound is:
questions.x: The band near 1730 cm⁻¹ shows a C=O, and the absence of any broad band rules out O–H, which all three other compounds contain. The acid would show the very broad 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ O–H band; that is the tempting choice if only the C=O band is read.

questions.q: Nitrogen dioxide released into the air contributes to acid rain mainly by forming:
questions.x: NO₂ reacts with oxygen and water in clouds: 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃. Sulphuric acid comes from SO₂, not from nitrogen oxides.

questions.q: In a microcomputer, the whole CPU is built on a single chip. This chip is called a:
questions.x: A microprocessor is a CPU made on one integrated-circuit chip. The motherboard is the main circuit board on which the microprocessor and other parts are mounted, not the CPU chip itself.

questions.q: Which type of ROM is supplied blank and can be programmed by the user only once?
questions.x: PROM (programmable ROM) can be written once and then cannot be changed. EPROM and EEPROM can be erased and reprogrammed, and mask ROM is written by the maker during manufacture, not by the user.

questions.q: When binary is converted to octal by grouping, each octal digit stands for a group of how many bits?
questions.x: 8 = 2³, so each octal digit matches exactly 3 bits. Groups of 4 bits are used for hexadecimal, because 16 = 2⁴.

questions.q: Where is a computer's MAC address normally stored?
o: In its network interface card, set by the maker
In the DNS server of the Internet
In the router's list of websites
questions.x: The MAC address is a physical address built into the NIC during manufacture. The IP address, not the MAC address, is the one a network or DNS deals with.

questions.q: A network made by joining two or more different topologies, for example several star networks linked to one bus cable, has which topology?
questions.x: Combining different topologies in one network gives a hybrid topology. A pure bus would have every computer tapped onto the one cable, without the star parts.

questions.q: What does NIC stand for in networking?
questions.x: A NIC is a Network Interface Card, the hardware that connects a computer to a network. Each NIC has its own MAC address.

questions.q: An employee copies his company's customer list onto a USB drive so that he can sell it to a rival firm. What is this?
questions.x: Taking an organisation's data without permission to sell it is data theft. A backup is made for the owner's use, not to give data to others.

questions.q: A cloud provider charges Rs 20 per server per hour. A shop uses 3 servers for 10 hours during a sale and then 1 server for the remaining 14 hours of the day. What is the cost for that day?
questions.x: 3 × 10 × 20 = Rs 600 for the sale hours and 1 × 14 × 20 = Rs 280 afterwards, total Rs 880. Rs 1 440 wrongly charges 3 servers for all 24 hours; paying only for use is the point of pay-as-you-go.

questions.q: An airline's booking computer updates its seat records the moment a seat is sold, so the same seat cannot be sold twice from offices in different cities. This is:
questions.x: A real-time reservation system updates the central records immediately, so every office sees the current seats. Batch processing would collect bookings and process them later, allowing double sales.

questions.q: The file `cv.docx` has the path `C:\Users\Ali\Docs\cv.docx`. Which folder is the parent folder of `Docs`?
questions.x: Each backslash separates a folder from the one inside it, so `Docs` sits directly inside `Ali`, whose path is `C:\Users\Ali`. `C:\Users` is the parent of `Ali`, one level higher.

questions.q: A report's header must appear on every page except the cover page (page 1). Which header setting should be used?
o: A page break after the cover
Deleting the header text on page 1
questions.x: Different First Page gives page 1 its own (empty) header while the other pages keep the normal one. Deleting the header on page 1 would remove it from every page, because all pages share it.

questions.q: Which order of database design steps is correct?
o: Physical design → logical design → conceptual design
Conceptual design → logical design → physical design
Logical design → conceptual design → physical design
Conceptual design → physical design → logical design
questions.x: Design moves from the DBMS-independent ER model (conceptual), to tables (logical), to storage details on the chosen DBMS (physical). Storage cannot be planned before the tables are known.

questions.q: Which of these is information rather than raw data?
o: The marks 67, 72 and 81 typed in from answer sheets
A list of roll numbers copied from the register
The scores read from quiz sheets before any working
The class average of 73 worked out from all the marks
questions.x: Information is data that has been processed into a meaningful result, such as an average. Marks, scores or roll numbers as they are first typed in are raw data that has not been processed yet.

questions.q: In the relational model, what is a table formally called?
questions.x: In relational terms a table is a relation, a row is a tuple and a column is an attribute. A domain is the set of allowed values of an attribute.

questions.q: A field is set as the primary key of an Access table. Which entry will Access refuse in that field?
o: A value typed in capital letters
A value already used in another record
A value entered through a form
A value entered in Datasheet View
questions.x: A primary key must be unique (and not empty), so a value that already exists in another record is refused. How the value is typed or where it is entered does not matter.

questions.q: What does a header file such as `stdio.h` mainly contain?
o: Declarations of library functions such as printf, and macro definitions
The complete machine code of printf and scanf
The main() function of every program
The finished executable file of the program
questions.x: A header file is source text with function declarations (prototypes) and macros. The machine code of printf is in the compiled library, which the linker joins to the program.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.1f", 2.5e2);
```
questions.x: 2.5e2 means 2.5 × 10² = 250, printed with one decimal place as 250.0. 0.025 would be 2.5e-2.
&& has higher precedence than ||, so the first is 1 || (0 && 0) = 1 || 0 = 1. The brackets in the second force (1 || 0) first, giving 1 && 0 = 0.

questions.q: In C, when is the condition of an `if` statement treated as false?
o: When its value is anything other than 1
When it uses a relational operator
questions.x: C treats 0 as false and every non-zero value, negative ones included, as true. So a condition such as -3 is true, not false.
%s reads the word Sara (it stops at the space) and %d reads the number 85 into m. m + 5 is added as numbers, giving 90, not joined as text (855).
d = 2: 27 % 2 = 1, go on. d = 3: 27 % 3 = 0, so prime = 0 and break leaves the loop with d still 3. 1 6 is what would print if no divisor were found (the loop stops when 6 * 6 > 27).

questions.q: A college wants the views of all its 600 students on a new online fee portal before the design starts, and it has only one week. Which way of gathering requirements suits this best?
o: A one-to-one interview with every student
Writing the program first and asking students afterwards
Watching one student at the fee counter for a day
An online questionnaire sent to every student
questions.x: A questionnaire collects answers from a large group quickly and cheaply. Interviews give detail but 600 of them cannot be done in a week, and one student's view is too small a sample.

questions.q: A project has two tasks done one after the other: design needs 6 person-months of work and coding needs 12 person-months. The same team of 3 programmers works on each task in turn, and the work divides evenly among them. How long does the project take?
questions.x: Design takes 6 / 3 = 2 months and coding 12 / 3 = 4 months, one after the other: 2 + 4 = 6 months. 18 months forgets to share the work among the three programmers; 4 months counts only the coding.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print(17 % 5 * 2 + 1)
```
questions.x: `%` and `*` have the same precedence and work left to right: 17 % 5 = 2, then 2 * 2 = 4, then 4 + 1 = 5. 6 comes from wrongly doing 17 % (5 * 2 + 1) = 17 % 11.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print(len(str(2 ** 10)))
```
questions.x: `2 ** 10` is 1024; `str` turns it into the text "1024", which has 4 characters. 1024 is the value itself, not its length.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
s = "  ecat  "
print(len(s.strip()))
```
questions.x: `strip()` removes the spaces at both ends, leaving "ecat", whose length is 4. 8 is the length before stripping; `strip` does not remove letters.

questions.q: Why does binary search need far fewer comparisons than linear search on a long sorted list?
o: It compares two elements at a time instead of one
Each comparison removes about half of the remaining elements
It starts from the last element instead of the first
It sorts the list again while searching
questions.x: Comparing with the middle element tells binary search which half can hold the target, so the part left to search halves each step (about log₂ n steps). It still makes one comparison at a time.

questions.q: To work out travel time, a route-planning program keeps only each road's length and speed limit and ignores details such as the colour of road signs. Which computational thinking skill is this?
questions.x: Keeping the details that matter and leaving out the rest is abstraction. Decomposition would mean breaking the problem into smaller sub-problems.

questions.q: A test of a new teaching method gives p = 0.002. What does this small p-value mean?
o: There is a 0.2% chance that the method works
The sample was too small to use
A result like this would be very unlikely if H₀ were true, so it is strong evidence against H₀
questions.x: The p-value is the chance of getting a result at least this extreme if H₀ were true; 0.002 is tiny, so H₀ is doubtful. It is not the chance that the method works.

questions.q: In a business plan, what is the executive summary?
o: A short overview of the whole plan, placed at its start
A detailed list of every expense
The CVs of all the employees
A list of references at the end
questions.x: The executive summary briefly states the idea, market, team and finances so a reader such as an investor gets the whole picture first. Detailed costs belong in the financial section.

questions.q: What is the passage chiefly about?
o: how the narrator learned to play cricket more carefully
why Mr Qureshi was angry with the narrator's friends
how the narrator came to own up to a mistake he had tried to hide
how the narrator saved up for a new bat
questions.x: After running away, the narrator writes a letter that "simply said what I had done" and delivers it himself. Mr Qureshi "did not look angry", and no bat is bought.

questions.q: Why did the narrator tear up his first two drafts?
o: They were too long for Mr Qureshi to read
They were full of excuses instead of a plain admission
His friends told him not to send them
He had spelt Mr Qureshi's name wrongly
questions.x: The drafts "were full of excuses about the wind and the uneven ground"; the third "simply said what I had done". The passage says nothing about length, friends or spelling.

questions.q: What Mr Qureshi said on the doorstep suggests that he:
o: had not known who broke the window
had planned to complain to the narrator's parents
had chosen to give the narrator the chance to own up himself
was angry that the narrator's friends had not come
questions.x: He "had known it was me all along" yet waited "to see whether I would come", so he deliberately left the step to the boy. Not knowing is contradicted by his own words.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the phrase "wore me down" most nearly means:
o: slowly tired me and weakened my resistance
questions.x: After days of watching the tired neighbour and waiting, the narrator gave in and wrote the letter, so the silence slowly weakened him. Damaging clothes takes "wore" literally.

questions.q: By calling the experience "the most expensive lesson of my childhood, and the cheapest", the narrator shows that he:
o: regrets having paid for the glass at all
is unsure how much the glass really cost
is still angry that he was made to pay
sees it as costly in money but worth far more than he paid
questions.x: Four months of pocket money was a lot for a boy, yet the lesson was cheap for what it taught. Nothing in the passage suggests regret or anger; he offered to pay himself.

questions.q: The writer's main purpose is to:
o: describe how satellites forecast the weather
explain the danger of debris in space and why it is hard to clear
argue that countries should stop launching satellites
explain how rockets carry satellites into orbit
questions.x: The passage sets out "the worry" about collisions, the "remedies" being tried and "The deeper difficulty" of paying for them. It never calls for an end to launches.

questions.q: Which of these is mentioned as a way of dealing with the problem?
o: Designing satellites to burn up in the atmosphere when they stop working
Painting satellites to protect them from fragments
Moving old satellites into the busiest orbits
questions.x: The third paragraph says satellites "are now designed to burn up in the atmosphere at the end of their working lives". Old satellites go to "graveyard" orbits "far from the crowded lanes", not the busiest ones.

questions.q: Based on the last paragraph, a company might be unwilling to pay for cleaning space mainly because:
o: debris does no harm to its own satellites
every cleaning method has been shown not to work
the rubbish will soon burn up on its own
others who paid nothing would gain from it just as much
questions.x: Cleaning "costs money while benefiting everyone, including those who paid nothing", so a payer gets no special return. The methods are not said to fail; none is "yet cheap enough to use widely".

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the phrase "in principle" most nearly means:
o: as a matter of moral rule
in theory, even if it may not happen in practice
questions.x: Debris "could, in principle, go on multiplying" describes something possible in theory, which the word "could" also signals. "With complete certainty" is too strong.

questions.q: In the second paragraph, the word "This" in "This is the worry" refers to:
o: the cost of launching new satellites
the loss of a tool by an astronaut
the way one collision creates fragments that can wreck other satellites
the speed of a bullet fired from a rifle
questions.x: The first paragraph ends with a fragment that can "wreck a working satellite" and a wreck that "becomes thousands of new fragments"; the next sentence explains "Every collision makes another collision more likely". The rifle bullet is only used to show the speed.
